## Statement

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{f\tilde p\ne0\}$ and $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are IID with law $Q$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The densities, integrability, support, and IID sampling hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-importance-sampling]]: With $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and $Y_i=0$ otherwise, the estimator is $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$.

[F2] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: For a random element $X$ with law $Q$, a nonnegative measurable $g$ satisfies $\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int g\,dQ$, possibly with value $+\infty$; if $g(X)$ is integrable, the same identity holds as a finite integral.

[F3] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: The Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions; in particular, the expectation of a finite average of integrable random variables is the average of their expectations.

[F4] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: The expectation of an integrable real random variable is its finite Lebesgue integral.

## Proof

**Given:** Use the target expectation $\theta:=\int f\,d\pi$ and the estimator specified in [[alg-importance-sampling]].

1.1 For every $i$, apply the nonnegative case of [F2] to $|Y_i|$. Since $X_i$ has law $Q$,
$$\mathbb E_Q|Y_i|=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{|f(x)|\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu\le\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\mathsf X}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Thus $Y_i$ is $Q$-integrable, so the integrable case of [F2] gives
$$\mathbb E_Q[Y_i]=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}f\tilde p\,d\mu.$$
The support condition makes $f\tilde p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$; hence this last integral equals $Z_p^{-1}\int_{\mathsf X}f\tilde p\,d\mu=\int f\,d\pi=\theta$. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Apply [F3] and step 1.1 to obtain $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_Q[Y_i]=\theta$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\tilde p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$ be measurable densities with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$ and $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and set $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$ and $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. For the ordinary importance sampling estimator in [[alg-importance-sampling]],
$$\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\int f\,d\pi.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The densities, integrability, support, and IID sampling hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[alg-importance-sampling]]: With $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and $Y_i=0$ otherwise, the estimator is $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$.

[F4] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]: The expectation of an integrable real random variable is its finite Lebesgue integral.

[F5] [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]: for a nonnegative measurable density $r$ and nonnegative measurable $h$, $\int h\,d(r\,d\mu)=\int hr\,d\mu$, including infinite values. [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]: an absolutely integrable real function has integral equal to the finite difference of the integrals of its positive and negative parts.

## Proof

**Given:** Use the target expectation $\theta:=\int f\,d\pi$ and the estimator specified in [[alg-importance-sampling]].

1.1 Use [F5] with density $r=q$ for integration against $Q$ and with $r=\tilde p/Z_p$ for integration against $\pi$. For every $i$, apply the nonnegative case of [F2] to $|Y_i|$. Since $X_i$ has law $Q$,
$$\mathbb E_Q|Y_i|=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{|f(x)|\tilde p(x)}{Z_pq(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\{q>0\}}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu\le\frac1{Z_p}\int_{\mathsf X}|f|\tilde p\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

## Statement

Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This conclusion is choice-free. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integrable ordinary importance sampling setup from [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]], plus $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$. Assume AC only for the CLT conclusion.

[F1] [[alg-importance-sampling]]: The estimate is the sample average of the weighted values $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$, with value $0$ when $q(X_i)=0$; the algorithm also establishes that this piecewise weighted-integrand map is measurable.

[F2] [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]: Under its support and integrability hypotheses, $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\theta=\int f\,d\pi$.

[F3] [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]: Applying measurable coordinatewise maps to an independent family preserves independence.

[F4] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: IID means a common law and mutual independence.

[F5] [[thm-iid-monte-carlo-mean-moments]]: For real IID $Y_i$ with finite first absolute moment, $\mathbb E\bar Y_n=\mathbb EY_1$; if $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)/n$.

[F6] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: For a nonnegative measurable function of a random element with law $Q$, expectation equals its integral against $Q$.

[F7] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]: For square-integrable real $Y$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb E Y)^2]$.

[F8] [[thm-iid-monte-carlo-central-limit]]: Under AC, a real IID sample with positive finite variance satisfies $\sqrt n(\bar Y_n-\mathbb EY_1)\Rightarrow N(0,\operatorname{Var}(Y_1))$.

[F9] [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]: A nonnegative measurable function has integral zero exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere.

[F10] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: $N(m,0)$ is the Dirac law $\delta_m$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC asserts that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; it is assumed only for the central limit conclusion.

## Proof

**Given:** The weighted values $Y_i$ from the Statement and the finite second moment $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$.

1.1 By [F1], each $Y_i$ is obtained from $X_i$ by the same measurable weighted-integrand map and $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Since the $X_i$ are IID, [F3] preserves independence and their common law under this map; [F4] therefore makes $(Y_i)$ IID. [F1, F3, F4, given]

2.1 By [F2], $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\theta$. Since $|y|\le1+y^2$, the finite second moment makes $Y_1$ integrable. Then [F5] gives $\mathbb E_Q[\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}]=\mathbb E_QY_1$ and $\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\sigma^2/n$, so $\mathbb E_QY_1=\theta$. [F2, F5, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Applying [F6] to the nonnegative squared weighted integrand gives $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]=Z_p^{-2}\int_{\{q>0\}}f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2/q(x)\,d\mu(x)$. By [F7] and step 2.1, $\sigma^2=\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]-\theta^2$, proving the displayed variance formula. [F1, F6, F7, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Assume AC as in [A1]. If $\sigma^2>0$, [F8] applies to the IID sequence from step 1.1 with mean $\theta$ from step 2.1 and yields the stated normal limit. If $\sigma^2=0$, [F7] gives $\mathbb E_Q[(Y_1-\theta)^2]=0$, so [F9] implies $Y_1=\theta$ $Q$-almost surely. By the common-law conclusion of step 1.1, each event $\{Y_i\ne\theta\}$ is null; for each fixed $n$, the union of the first $n$ such events is null. Thus $\bar Y_n=\theta$ almost surely for each $n$, and the centered sample mean has law $\delta_0=N(0,0)$ for every $n$ by [F10]. The variance argument in the preceding steps used no choice axiom. [A1, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$

$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$

## Statement

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space, $\tilde p\ge0$ a measurable target density with $Z_p=\int\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$, and $q\ge0$ a measurable proposal probability density with $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. Suppose
$$\mathbb E_QW_1=Z_p\in(0,\infty),\qquad \mathbb E_Q[W_1|f(X_1)|]<\infty.$$
Then the self-normalized estimate in [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]] satisfies
$$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n}\longrightarrow\theta:=\int f\,d\pi\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
On a finite prefix where all observed weights vanish, the algorithm's no-estimate status is interpreted as the value $0$ for this convergence statement; almost surely that fallback is eventually unnecessary.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The target, proposal, support, integrability, and IID sampling assumptions in the Statement.

[F4] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: IID means mutual independence and a common law; no moment condition is included in the definition.

[F5] [[thm-iid-monte-carlo-mean-consistency]]: For real IID $Y_i$ with finite first absolute moment, their sample mean converges almost surely to $\mathbb EY_1$.

[F7] [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]: A nonnegative measurable function has integral zero over a measurable null set.

**Given:** Use $W_i$ and $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n}$ from the Statement and [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]].

## Statement

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$, $\tilde p$, $Z_p$, $\pi$, $q$, $Q$, $f$, and $W_i$ satisfy the hypotheses and definitions of [[thm-self-normalized-importance-sampling-is-consistent-under-finite-moments]]. Assume also
$$\mathbb E_Q[W_1^2]<\infty,\qquad \mathbb E_Q[(W_1f(X_1))^2]<\infty,$$
and assume AC for the central limit conclusion. Set $\theta=\int f\,d\pi$ and
$$\tau^2:=\frac1{Z_p^2}\mathbb E_Q\!\left[W_1^2(f(X_1)-\theta)^2\right].$$
This is finite under the stated second moments. Then the estimate in [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]] satisfies
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2).$$
Define its plug-in variance estimate, when $S_n=\sum_iW_i>0$, by
$$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{MC}}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n}):=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^2(f(X_i)-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n})^2}{S_n^2},$$
and set this quantity to $0$ if $S_n=0$. Then, without using AC,
$$n\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{MC}}(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n})\longrightarrow\tau^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
Define $\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\mathrm{MC},n}$ to be the nonnegative square root of this plug-in variance. Then $\sqrt n\,\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\mathrm{MC},n}\to\tau$ almost surely. No finite-sample unbiasedness assertion is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The IID sampling and first-moment hypotheses of [[thm-self-normalized-importance-sampling-is-consistent-under-finite-moments]], the additional second moments, and AC for the CLT branch.

[F1] [[alg-self-normalized-importance-sampling]]: The algorithm defines a measurable weight $w$ and, for $S_n>0$, returns $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{SN},n}=\sum_iW_if(X_i)/S_n$; when $S_n=0$, it returns the status **no estimate: zero observed target weight**.

[F2] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: A nonnegative measurable function of an IID draw with law $Q$ has expectation given by integration against $Q$, possibly with value $+\infty$; the same identity holds as a finite integral for integrable functions.

[F3] [[thm-multivariate-iid-central-limit-theorem]]: Under AC, IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued variables with finite second moment and covariance $\Sigma$ have sample-mean limit $\sqrt n(\bar X_n-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma)$; singular $\Sigma$ is allowed.

[F4] [[thm-first-and-second-order-delta-method-for-random-vectors]]: If $\sqrt n(T_n-\eta)\Rightarrow Z$ and $g(\eta+h)-g(\eta)=Ah+o(\|h\|)$, then $\sqrt n(g(T_n)-g(\eta))\Rightarrow AZ$.

[F5] [[thm-self-normalized-importance-sampling-is-consistent-under-finite-moments]]: Under its support and finite first-moment assumptions, the ratio estimate converges almost surely to $\theta$, and its denominator is eventually positive almost surely. For the convergence statement, that theorem interprets the algorithm's no-estimate status as the numeric value $0$ on any finite prefix with zero observed target weight.

[F6] [[thm-kolmogorov-iid-l1-strong-law]]: Every IID integrable real sequence has sample mean converging almost surely to its expectation.

[F7] [[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]]: Applying one measurable function to each member of an independent family preserves independence.

[F8] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: A family is IID when it is mutually independent and has a common law.

[F9] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]: Covariance is the expectation of the product of centered square-integrable variables, and variance is the self-covariance.

[F10] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: Under AC, $Z\sim N_d(0,\Sigma)$ exactly when each linear projection $u\cdot Z$ is normal with variance $u^T\Sigma u$; singular covariance is allowed.

[F11] [[cor-holder-inequality-for-random-variables]]: For conjugate exponents $p=q=2$, square-integrable real random variables $R,S$ satisfy $\mathbb E|RS|\le(\mathbb E|R|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E|S|^2)^{1/2}$, so $RS$ is integrable.

[F12] [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]: Finite products and sums, and absolute values, of measurable real functions remain measurable.

[F13] [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]: A nonnegative measurable function has integral zero over a measurable null set.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC asserts that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; the CLT branch inherits it through [F3] and [F10], while the strong-law standard-error branch is choice-free.

$$\mathbb E_Q[W_i|f(X_i)|]=\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{\tilde p(x)|f(x)|}{q(x)}q(x)\,d\mu(x)=\int_{\{q>0\}}\tilde p|f|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Full proposal support and finite target variance of $f$ are sufficient for ordinary importance sampling to have finite estimator variance.

## Facts & Assumptions

$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
